cards.def: First word of a sentence.
cards.name: <u>Kangaroos</u> are native to Australia.

cards.def: First word of a direct quotation.
cards.name: Melinda said, “<u>You’re</u> my best friend.”

cards.def: A person’s name or nickname.
cards.name: <u>Peggy</u> likes to be called <u>Peg</u>.

cards.def: A relationship word used in place of a person’s name.
cards.name: <u>Mom</u> and <u>Dad</u> went out to dinner.

cards.def: Initials.
cards.name: Eddie Trujilo’s friends call him <u>E.T.</u>

cards.def: People’s titles and their abbreviations.
cards.name: My dentist’s name is <u>Doctor</u> Olson.

cards.def: People’s titles and their abbreviations.
cards.name: My dentist’s name is <u>Dr.</u> Olson.

cards.def: Names of places, cities, states, roads, and avenues.
cards.name: <u>Disney World</u> is in <u>Orlando</u>, <u>Florida</u>.

cards.def: Names of places, cities, states, roads, and avenues.
cards.name: I live on <u>Fifth Street</u> and <u>Marble Road</u>.

cards.def: Names of groups.
cards.name: Jenny is a <u>Girl Scout</u> leader.

cards.def: Days of the week, months of the year, and holidays.
cards.name: My birthday is on <u>Tuesday</u>, <u>May</u> 8.

cards.def: Days of the week, months of the year, and holidays.
cards.name: We’re going camping on <u>Labor Day</u>.

cards.def: Titles of books, movies, games, and magazines.
cards.name: <u>Adventures of Tom Sawyer</u> is a good book.

cards.def: Titles of books, movies, games, and magazines.
cards.name: We watched <u>The Chronicles of Narnia</u>.

cards.def: Titles of books, movies, games, and magazines.
cards.name: Jesse likes to play <u>Madden NFL</u> with his friends.

cards.def: Names of planets and stars. (sun and moon are exceptions)
cards.name: The smallest planet is <u>Mercury</u>.

cards.def: Names of planets and stars. (sun and moon are exceptions)
cards.name: The <u>Big Dipper</u> is part of the constellation <u>Ursa Major</u>.

cards.def: Countries, languages, and nationalities.
cards.name: When I visited <u>France</u>, I spoke <u>French</u>.

cards.def: Countries, languages, and nationalities.
cards.name: My grandparents are <u>German</u>.

cards.def: The pronoun I.
cards.name: Malachi and <u>I</u> went fishing today.

cards.def: First word in the greeting of a letter or e-mail.
cards.name: <u>Dear</u> Uncle Bill,

cards.def: First word in the closing of a letter or e-mail.
cards.name: <u>Your</u> nephew, Jason

cards.def: Compass points when they name a specific region.
cards.name: Summers in the <u>Southwest</u> can be very hot.

cards.def: Compass points when they name a specific region.
cards.name: Australia is in the <u>Southern Hemisphere</u>.

cards.def: Acronyms — a word formed from the first letter of a series of words.
cards.name: Everybody needs some <u>TLC</u>.

cards.def: Acronyms — a word formed from the first letter of a series of words.
cards.name: I must do my homework <u>ASAP</u>, or I can’t go outside.

cards.def: Acronyms — a word formed from the first letter of a series of words.
cards.name: Dad uses the <u>ATM</u> at our bank.

cards.def: Period — to end a sentence.
cards.name: Abraham Lincoln was born in Kentucky.

cards.def: Period — after an abbreviation.
cards.name: Fri. Aug. Ln. Mrs. Dr. U.S.

cards.def: Period — after a person’s initials.
cards.name: Roger Smith’s initials are R.S.

cards.def: Question mark — after a question.
cards.name: Will you wait for me?

cards.def: Exclamation mark — after a word or sentence that shows strong feeling.
cards.name: Run! Nanook, run!

cards.def: Exclamation mark — after a word or sentence that shows strong feeling.
cards.name: I won the race!

cards.def: Comma — to separate words in a series.
cards.name: Raymond likes football, soccer, and hockey.

cards.def: Comma — to separate the day of the month from the year.
cards.name: June 25, 2010

cards.def: Comma — to separate the day of the month from the year.
cards.name: March 3, 1865

cards.def: Comma — to separate a street address, city, and state.
cards.name: Queens, New York

cards.def: Comma — to separate a street address, city, and state.
cards.name: 75 Rainier Lane, Rochester, New Hampshire

cards.def: Comma — in a friendly letter after the greeting.
cards.name: Dear Susie,

cards.def: Comma — in a friendly letter after the greeting.
cards.name: Hi Uncle Fred,

cards.def: Comma — in a friendly letter following the closing.
cards.name: Love,

cards.def: Comma — in a friendly letter following the closing.
cards.name: Yours truly,

cards.def: Comma — before a conjunction (and, but, or, so) to join two simple sentences.
cards.name: We were late, so we missed the concert.

cards.def: Comma — to separate the speaker from a direct quotation.
cards.name: Jacob asked, “Where do you live?”

cards.def: Quotation marks — at the beginning and end of a direct quotation.
cards.name: “Do your homework,” Mr. Douglas said.

cards.def: Quotation marks — at the beginning and end of a direct quotation.
cards.name: Dad asked, “Will you take out the trash?”

cards.def: Apostrophe — in a contraction, to show where letters are left out.
cards.name: I didn’t go to school today.

cards.def: Apostrophe — to show possession (singular and plural nouns).
cards.name: That is the cat’s food.

cards.def: Apostrophe — to show possession (singular and plural nouns).
cards.name: These are my friends’ bikes.

cards.def: Parentheses — to add information that is interesting but not very important.
cards.name: Our dog (a poodle) is brown and white.

cards.def: Parentheses — to add information that is interesting but not very important.
cards.name: We’re leaving (in my car) to visit a friend.

cards.def: Parentheses — to surround words or figures to make things clearer.
cards.name: Patrick earned six hundred dollars ($600) last week.

cards.def: Colon — to introduce a list of items.
cards.name: These are vegetables: carrots, celery, and lettuce.

cards.def: Colon — to separate hours and minutes.
cards.name: School starts at 7:30 a.m.

cards.def: Colon — after the greeting in a business letter.
cards.name: Dear Dr. Bennett:

cards.def: Semicolon — to join two complete sentences in place of a conjunction.
cards.name: Caprice stayed after school; she helped her teacher.

cards.def: Semicolon — to separate a series of items that already contain commas.
cards.name: The Coos County Fiddle competition winners are Sara James, Coquille; Teri Matthews, Myrtle Point; and John Lynns, North Bend.

cards.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
cards.name: Isaac hit <u>a</u> grand slam.

cards.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
cards.name: Carlotta has <u>a</u> new puppy.

cards.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
cards.name: Maria gave her mother <u>a</u> box of candy.

cards.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
cards.name: Jing saw <u>an</u> island out in the distance.

cards.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
cards.name: Abraham is <u>an</u> honest man.

cards.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
cards.name: I ate <u>an</u> apple and <u>an</u> orange for breakfast.

cards.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
cards.name: Landau is <u>the</u> most popular member of his team.

cards.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
cards.name: Bridget climbed <u>the</u> tallest tree in her backyard.

cards.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
cards.name: Daryl is <u>the</u> only uncle I have.

cards.def: A common noun is a general person, place, or thing; it begins with a lowercase letter.
cards.name: The <u>lake</u> was filled with <u>boats</u>.

cards.def: A common noun is a general person, place, or thing; it begins with a lowercase letter.
cards.name: The <u>girl</u> wore a blue <u>dress</u>.

cards.def: A proper noun is a specific person, place, or thing; it always begins with a capital letter.
cards.name: <u>Toni</u> lives in <u>Alaska</u>.

cards.def: A proper noun is a specific person, place, or thing; it always begins with a capital letter.
cards.name: The <u>Great Pyramid of Giza</u> is located in <u>Egypt</u>.

cards.def: A possessive noun shows ownership. Add ’s to make a singular or plural noun possessive.
cards.name: Ralph<u>’s</u> bicycle is bright red.

cards.def: A possessive noun shows ownership. Add ’s to make a singular or plural noun possessive.
cards.name: The children<u>’s</u> books are downstairs.

cards.def: If a noun already ends in s, add only an apostrophe (’) to make it possessive.
cards.name: Ms. Woods<u>’</u> grammar lessons are easy to understand.

cards.def: If a noun already ends in s, add only an apostrophe (’) to make it possessive.
cards.name: The lawyers<u>’</u> offices are on the third floor.

cards.def: A pronoun is a word used in place of one or more nouns.
cards.name: <u>They</u> went to the library today.  (They = Sue and Jake)

cards.def: A pronoun is a word used in place of one or more nouns.
cards.name: <u>He</u> borrowed his sister’s car.  (He = Ben)

cards.def: Use a noun OR a pronoun, but not both together, in a sentence.
cards.name: The fly landed on my food.  (not: The fly <u>it</u> landed on my food.)

cards.def: A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces. (mountain → it, not her)
cards.name: The mountain has lots of snow on <u>it</u>.

cards.def: A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces. (Bob → him, not it)
cards.name: Bob won! We were happy for <u>him</u>.

cards.def: Use a possessive pronoun WITH a noun: my, your, his, her, our, their.
cards.name: Chelsea is <u>my</u> dog.

cards.def: Use a possessive pronoun BY ITSELF: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
cards.name: Chelsea is <u>mine</u>.

cards.def: When there is more than one subject or object, put the first-person pronoun (I, me, we, us) last.
cards.name: Lucinda and <u>I</u> play the piano.

cards.def: When there is more than one subject or object, put the first-person pronoun (I, me, we, us) last.
cards.name: Dad tossed the ball to Pete and <u>me</u>.

cards.def: Use I when you are DOING the action.
cards.name: <u>I</u> missed the bus.

cards.def: Use me when you are RECEIVING the action.
cards.name: Nanook brought the bone to <u>me</u>.

cards.def: I or me? Add the invisible verb (do): ‘Beth swims better than I (do).’
cards.name: Beth swims better than <u>I</u> (do).

cards.def: I or me? When in doubt, leave the other person out: ‘The cat scratched me.’ (not I)
cards.name: The cat scratched <u>me</u>.

cards.def: Use myself only after you have used I in the sentence.
cards.name: I had to prepare the meal <u>myself</u>.

cards.def: Use myself only after you have used I in the sentence.
cards.name: I fixed <u>myself</u> a sandwich.

cards.def: Add -s to the end of most nouns to make them plural.
cards.name: boat → boat<u>s</u>   ·   flower → flower<u>s</u>

cards.def: Add -es to nouns ending in s, ss, sh, ch, x (and sometimes o).
cards.name: gas → gas<u>es</u>   ·   dish → dish<u>es</u>   ·   box → box<u>es</u>   ·   tomato → tomato<u>es</u>

cards.def: If a noun ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i and add -es.
cards.name: baby → bab<u>ies</u>   ·   strawberry → strawberr<u>ies</u>

cards.def: If a noun ends in a vowel + y, just add -s.
cards.name: donkey → donkey<u>s</u>   ·   monkey → monkey<u>s</u>

cards.def: Some nouns change completely when they become plural (irregular).
cards.name: man → <u>men</u>   ·   tooth → <u>teeth</u>   ·   mouse → <u>mice</u>   ·   foot → <u>feet</u>   ·   child → <u>children</u>

cards.def: Some nouns don’t change at all from singular to plural.
cards.name: fish → fish   ·   deer → deer   ·   sheep → sheep

cards.def: Past tense — the action already happened.
cards.name: Aunt Corena <u>baked</u> my favorite cookies yesterday.

cards.def: Present tense — the action is happening now.
cards.name: Aunt Corena <u>bakes</u> my favorite cookies.

cards.def: Future tense — the action will happen later.
cards.name: Aunt Corena <u>will bake</u> my favorite cookies tomorrow.

cards.def: Most verbs are regular — add -ed to make the past tense.
cards.name: walk → walk<u>ed</u>   ·   open → open<u>ed</u>   ·   start → start<u>ed</u>

cards.def: Irregular verbs don’t add -ed — the word itself changes in the past tense.
cards.name: go → <u>went</u>   ·   eat → <u>ate</u>   ·   take → <u>took</u>   ·   write → <u>wrote</u>   ·   become → <u>became</u>

cards.def: Use a singular verb with a singular subject. (boy → plays)
cards.name: The boy <u>plays</u> with trucks.

cards.def: Use a plural verb with a plural subject. (boys → play)
cards.name: The boys <u>play</u> with trucks.

cards.def: Two or more subjects joined by ‘and’ take a plural verb.
cards.name: Rita and Melanie <u>are</u> good tennis players.

cards.def: Two or more subjects joined by ‘and’ take a plural verb.
cards.name: He and she <u>were</u> the teams’ leaders.

cards.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
cards.name: Apple pie and ice cream <u>is</u> my favorite dessert.

cards.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
cards.name: Bacon and eggs <u>is</u> a popular combination.

cards.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
cards.name: Peanut butter and jelly <u>makes</u> a healthy sandwich.

cards.def: A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought. All sentences begin with a capital letter and end with a punctuation mark.
cards.name: Sentence

cards.chapter: Lesson 13 · New: Adjectives That Tell What Kind, Which One, and How Many; New: Diagramming Adjectives
cards.def: An adjective is a word that describes a noun or pronoun. Adjectives tell what kind, which one, how many, and whose.

cards.chapter: Lesson 14 · New: Adjectives That Tell Whose (Possessive Nouns and Pronouns); New: Articles
cards.def: If the noun is singular or an irregular plural, add an apostrophe and the letter s.
cards.name: Apostrophes: singular or irregular plural nouns

cards.chapter: Lesson 14 · New: Adjectives That Tell Whose (Possessive Nouns and Pronouns); New: Articles
cards.def: If the noun is plural and already ends in an s, simply add the apostrophe.

cards.chapter: Lesson 17 · New: Adverbs That Tell How and When; New: Diagramming Adverbs
cards.def: An adverb is a word that describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. Adverbs tell how, when, where, how often, and to what extent.
cards.name: Adverb

cards.name: List: Helping Verbs

cards.def: The noun or pronoun in the complete predicate that receives the action of the verb.
cards.name: Direct object

cards.chapter: Lesson 25 · New: Indirect Objects; Review: Direct Objects; Review: Subject and Object Pronouns
cards.def: The noun or pronoun that is between the action verb and the direct object of a sentence. It answers the question "to whom" or "for whom" the action is done.
cards.name: Indirect object

cards.chapter: Lesson 28 · New: Simple Versus Complete Subjects and Predicates; Review: Subjects, Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs, and Direct Objects
cards.def: The verb and other words that tell us what is said about the subject. It is the part of the sentence in which the verb is found.
cards.name: Complete predicate

cards.chapter: Lesson 28 · New: Simple Versus Complete Subjects and Predicates; Review: Subjects, Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs, and Direct Objects
cards.def: The simple subject and other words that tell us who or what the sentence is about. It is the part of the sentence in which the simple subject is found.
cards.name: Complete subject

cards.chapter: Lesson 28 · New: Simple Versus Complete Subjects and Predicates; Review: Subjects, Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs, and Direct Objects
cards.def: The main verb plus any helping verbs.
cards.name: Simple predicate

cards.chapter: Lesson 28 · New: Simple Versus Complete Subjects and Predicates; Review: Subjects, Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs, and Direct Objects
cards.def: The main word or term that tells us who or what the sentence is about.
cards.name: Simple subject

cards.def: A noun or pronoun in the complete predicate that renames the subject.
cards.name: Predicate nominative

cards.chapter: Lesson 32 · New: Predicate Adjectives; Review: Linking Verbs; Review: Predicate Nominatives
cards.def: An adjective in the complete predicate that describes the subject.
cards.name: Predicate adjective

cards.chapter: Lesson 35 · New: Four Types of Sentences; New: Conjugating the Verb “To Go”
cards.def: A sentence that shows sudden or strong feeling. An exclamation always ends with an exclamation point.
cards.name: Exclamation

cards.chapter: Lesson 35 · New: Four Types of Sentences; New: Conjugating the Verb “To Go”
cards.def: A sentence that gives information. Statements always end with a period.
cards.name: Statement

cards.chapter: Lesson 35 · New: Four Types of Sentences; New: Conjugating the Verb “To Go”
cards.def: The four different types of sentences are statements, commands, questions, and exclamations.
cards.name: Types of sentences

cards.chapter: Lesson 36 · New: Commands (with Diagramming); Review: Statements
cards.def: A sentence that gives an order or makes a request. A command sentence ends with either a period or an exclamation point.
cards.name: Command

cards.chapter: Lesson 37 · New: Questions (with Diagramming); Learn to Proofread: Insert a Question Mark
cards.def: A sentence that asks something. A question always ends with a question mark.
cards.name: Question

cards.chapter: Lesson 57 · New: Conjunctions; New: Compound Subjects, Compound Predicates, and Compound Sentences; New: Commas in a Series
cards.def: Two or more verbs that are joined by a conjunction and that have the same subject.
cards.name: Compound predicate

cards.chapter: Lesson 57 · New: Conjunctions; New: Compound Subjects, Compound Predicates, and Compound Sentences; New: Commas in a Series
cards.def: A subject with two or more parts that are joined by a conjunction.
cards.name: Compound subject

cards.chapter: Lesson 57 · New: Conjunctions; New: Compound Subjects, Compound Predicates, and Compound Sentences; New: Commas in a Series

cards.chapter: Lesson 57 · New: Conjunctions; New: Compound Subjects, Compound Predicates, and Compound Sentences; New: Commas in a Series
cards.def: Use a comma before a conjunction in a compound sentence.
cards.name: Compound sentences: comma

cards.def: Use a comma to separate an introductory element from the rest of a sentence.
cards.name: Introductory elements: comma

cards.name: Contraction

cards.chapter: Lesson 60 · New: Contractions; Review: Personal Pronouns; Review: Adjectives
cards.def: Use an apostrophe to show where letters have been omitted in a contraction.
cards.name: Apostrophes: contractions

cards.chapter: Lesson 63 · New: Direct Quotations at the End of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences
cards.def: The exact words that someone says. Direct quotations are always enclosed by quotation marks.
cards.name: Direct quotation

cards.chapter: Lesson 63 · New: Direct Quotations at the End of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences
cards.def: The exact words a person says are always enclosed by quotation marks.
cards.name: Quotation at the end: quotation marks

cards.chapter: Lesson 63 · New: Direct Quotations at the End of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences
cards.def: Direct quotations begin with a capital letter.
cards.name: Quotation at the end: capital letter

cards.chapter: Lesson 63 · New: Direct Quotations at the End of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences
cards.def: The quotation is separated from the rest of the sentence by a comma.
cards.name: Quotation at the end: comma

cards.chapter: Lesson 63 · New: Direct Quotations at the End of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences
cards.def: The end punctuation mark always comes inside the closing quotation mark.
cards.name: Quotation at the end: end mark

cards.chapter: Lesson 64 · New: Direct Quotations at the Beginning of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences
cards.def: The exact words a person says are always enclosed by quotation marks.
cards.name: Quotation at the beginning: quotation marks

cards.chapter: Lesson 64 · New: Direct Quotations at the Beginning of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences
cards.def: Direct quotations begin with a capital letter.
cards.name: Quotation at the beginning: capital letter

cards.chapter: Lesson 64 · New: Direct Quotations at the Beginning of Sentences; Review: Four Types of Sentences

41.def: Comma — in a friendly letter following the closing.
41.name: Yours truly,

42.def: Comma — before a conjunction (and, but, or, so) to join two simple sentences.
42.name: We were late, so we missed the concert.

43.def: Comma — to separate the speaker from a direct quotation.
43.name: Jacob asked, “Where do you live?”

44.def: Quotation marks — at the beginning and end of a direct quotation.
44.name: “Do your homework,” Mr. Douglas said.

45.def: Quotation marks — at the beginning and end of a direct quotation.
45.name: Dad asked, “Will you take out the trash?”

46.def: Apostrophe — in a contraction, to show where letters are left out.
46.name: I didn’t go to school today.

47.def: Apostrophe — to show possession (singular and plural nouns).
47.name: That is the cat’s food.

48.def: Apostrophe — to show possession (singular and plural nouns).
48.name: These are my friends’ bikes.

49.def: Parentheses — to add information that is interesting but not very important.
49.name: Our dog (a poodle) is brown and white.

50.def: Parentheses — to add information that is interesting but not very important.
50.name: We’re leaving (in my car) to visit a friend.

51.def: Parentheses — to surround words or figures to make things clearer.
51.name: Patrick earned six hundred dollars ($600) last week.

52.def: Colon — to introduce a list of items.
52.name: These are vegetables: carrots, celery, and lettuce.

53.def: Colon — to separate hours and minutes.
53.name: School starts at 7:30 a.m.

54.def: Colon — after the greeting in a business letter.
54.name: Dear Dr. Bennett:

55.def: Semicolon — to join two complete sentences in place of a conjunction.
55.name: Caprice stayed after school; she helped her teacher.

56.def: Semicolon — to separate a series of items that already contain commas.
56.name: The Coos County Fiddle competition winners are Sara James, Coquille; Teri Matthews, Myrtle Point; and John Lynns, North Bend.

57.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
57.name: Isaac hit <u>a</u> grand slam.

58.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
58.name: Carlotta has <u>a</u> new puppy.

59.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
59.name: Maria gave her mother <u>a</u> box of candy.

60.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
60.name: Jing saw <u>an</u> island out in the distance.

61.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
61.name: Abraham is <u>an</u> honest man.

62.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
62.name: I ate <u>an</u> apple and <u>an</u> orange for breakfast.

63.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
63.name: Landau is <u>the</u> most popular member of his team.

64.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
64.name: Bridget climbed <u>the</u> tallest tree in her backyard.

65.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
65.name: Daryl is <u>the</u> only uncle I have.

66.def: A common noun is a general person, place, or thing; it begins with a lowercase letter.
66.name: The <u>lake</u> was filled with <u>boats</u>.

67.def: A common noun is a general person, place, or thing; it begins with a lowercase letter.
67.name: The <u>girl</u> wore a blue <u>dress</u>.

68.def: A proper noun is a specific person, place, or thing; it always begins with a capital letter.
68.name: <u>Toni</u> lives in <u>Alaska</u>.

69.def: A proper noun is a specific person, place, or thing; it always begins with a capital letter.
69.name: The <u>Great Pyramid of Giza</u> is located in <u>Egypt</u>.

70.def: A possessive noun shows ownership. Add ’s to make a singular or plural noun possessive.
70.name: Ralph<u>’s</u> bicycle is bright red.

71.def: A possessive noun shows ownership. Add ’s to make a singular or plural noun possessive.
71.name: The children<u>’s</u> books are downstairs.

72.def: If a noun already ends in s, add only an apostrophe (’) to make it possessive.
72.name: Ms. Woods<u>’</u> grammar lessons are easy to understand.

73.def: If a noun already ends in s, add only an apostrophe (’) to make it possessive.
73.name: The lawyers<u>’</u> offices are on the third floor.

74.def: A pronoun is a word used in place of one or more nouns.
74.name: <u>They</u> went to the library today.  (They = Sue and Jake)

75.def: A pronoun is a word used in place of one or more nouns.
75.name: <u>He</u> borrowed his sister’s car.  (He = Ben)

76.def: Use a noun OR a pronoun, but not both together, in a sentence.
76.name: The fly landed on my food.  (not: The fly <u>it</u> landed on my food.)

77.def: A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces. (mountain → it, not her)
77.name: The mountain has lots of snow on <u>it</u>.

78.def: A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces. (Bob → him, not it)
78.name: Bob won! We were happy for <u>him</u>.

79.def: Use a possessive pronoun WITH a noun: my, your, his, her, our, their.
79.name: Chelsea is <u>my</u> dog.

80.def: Use a possessive pronoun BY ITSELF: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
80.name: Chelsea is <u>mine</u>.

81.def: When there is more than one subject or object, put the first-person pronoun (I, me, we, us) last.
81.name: Lucinda and <u>I</u> play the piano.

82.def: When there is more than one subject or object, put the first-person pronoun (I, me, we, us) last.
82.name: Dad tossed the ball to Pete and <u>me</u>.

83.def: Use I when you are DOING the action.
83.name: <u>I</u> missed the bus.

84.def: Use me when you are RECEIVING the action.
84.name: Nanook brought the bone to <u>me</u>.

85.def: I or me? Add the invisible verb (do): ‘Beth swims better than I (do).’
85.name: Beth swims better than <u>I</u> (do).

86.def: I or me? When in doubt, leave the other person out: ‘The cat scratched me.’ (not I)
86.name: The cat scratched <u>me</u>.

87.def: Use myself only after you have used I in the sentence.
87.name: I had to prepare the meal <u>myself</u>.

88.def: Use myself only after you have used I in the sentence.
88.name: I fixed <u>myself</u> a sandwich.

89.def: Add -s to the end of most nouns to make them plural.
89.name: boat → boat<u>s</u>   ·   flower → flower<u>s</u>

90.def: Add -es to nouns ending in s, ss, sh, ch, x (and sometimes o).
90.name: gas → gas<u>es</u>   ·   dish → dish<u>es</u>   ·   box → box<u>es</u>   ·   tomato → tomato<u>es</u>

91.def: If a noun ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i and add -es.
91.name: baby → bab<u>ies</u>   ·   strawberry → strawberr<u>ies</u>

92.def: If a noun ends in a vowel + y, just add -s.
92.name: donkey → donkey<u>s</u>   ·   monkey → monkey<u>s</u>

93.def: Some nouns change completely when they become plural (irregular).
93.name: man → <u>men</u>   ·   tooth → <u>teeth</u>   ·   mouse → <u>mice</u>   ·   foot → <u>feet</u>   ·   child → <u>children</u>

94.def: Some nouns don’t change at all from singular to plural.
94.name: fish → fish   ·   deer → deer   ·   sheep → sheep

95.def: Past tense — the action already happened.
95.name: Aunt Corena <u>baked</u> my favorite cookies yesterday.

96.def: Present tense — the action is happening now.
96.name: Aunt Corena <u>bakes</u> my favorite cookies.

97.def: Future tense — the action will happen later.
97.name: Aunt Corena <u>will bake</u> my favorite cookies tomorrow.

98.def: Most verbs are regular — add -ed to make the past tense.
98.name: walk → walk<u>ed</u>   ·   open → open<u>ed</u>   ·   start → start<u>ed</u>

99.def: Irregular verbs don’t add -ed — the word itself changes in the past tense.
99.name: go → <u>went</u>   ·   eat → <u>ate</u>   ·   take → <u>took</u>   ·   write → <u>wrote</u>   ·   become → <u>became</u>

100.def: Use a singular verb with a singular subject. (boy → plays)
100.name: The boy <u>plays</u> with trucks.

101.def: Use a plural verb with a plural subject. (boys → play)
101.name: The boys <u>play</u> with trucks.

102.def: Two or more subjects joined by ‘and’ take a plural verb.
102.name: Rita and Melanie <u>are</u> good tennis players.

103.def: Two or more subjects joined by ‘and’ take a plural verb.
103.name: He and she <u>were</u> the teams’ leaders.

104.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
104.name: Apple pie and ice cream <u>is</u> my favorite dessert.

105.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
105.name: Bacon and eggs <u>is</u> a popular combination.

106.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
106.name: Peanut butter and jelly <u>makes</u> a healthy sandwich.
